idiom_name: hub struct with interface-typed colleagues; a goroutine hub on channels for asynchronous routing
implementation_notes: Go has no inheritance, so the mediator is a struct plus a small interface: define a Colleague interface (typically one Receive(Event) method), keep the participants in a slice or map inside the hub, and give the hub a Send/route method that decides who reacts; colleagues hold only the hub. Implicit interface satisfaction means any type can be a colleague without a base class, which is the pattern's structure with the ceremony removed. When colleagues must not block each other or the shared state needs a single owner, run the hub as a goroutine that receives events on a channel and never hands out its state - the canonical Go replacement for a locked shared object, share memory by communicating.
pitfalls: Interfaces are satisfied implicitly, so nothing stops a colleague from keeping a concrete peer and calling it directly; the hub is a convention enforced by review, not by the compiler.
A synchronous hub blocks its caller and can deadlock when a colleague sends back into it; for concurrent hubs use one owner goroutine with bounded channels and pass values instead of shared pointers.
Slices and maps of colleagues are not safe for concurrent registration: guard the hub with a mutex or confine registration to the hub goroutine via add/remove messages.
A typed-nil interface value compiles and panics on first call, so validate registrations.
